description.narrative: Sexual exploitation of children (SEC) is a grave violation of children’s rights and affects millions of children and youth annually, regardless of gender. No region, country or child is immune, though girls, boys and children with other gender identities face differing levels of risk to different manifestations of SEC depending on their intersectional vulnerability factors. It impacts heavily and long lastingly on their physical, emotional and mental well-being. It deprives children and youth of establishing healthy (sexual) relationships and from developing to the best of their potential. The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC and will work in 12 countries in Latin America and South and South East Asia: Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, India, Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Philippines and Thailand.

The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC by working towards the following long-term impact: “Children in all of their diversity are better protected from sexual exploitation.” This activity forms part of the SUFASEC programme. The long-term impact will be reached through three interlinking objectives that address different dimensions (social norms, assets/environments, and laws/policies/systems). 1. Children, youth and their communities successfully challenge social norms and harmful practices related to SEC 2. Children and youth have access to and are supported by strengthened assets and protective environments 3. Children and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved (implementation of) laws, policies, and systems

The different stakeholder groups involved in the SUFASEC programme include: - Children and youth in all their diversity: A child-centred approach: children and youth are the most important stakeholders. When children/youth fall victim to SEC the physical and mental impact can be long lasting. The Alliance adheres to the UN definition of child (0-18 years) and youth (15-24 years)- Caregivers and Communities: Critical stakeholders in the community include parents, caregivers, community leaders, teachers, local Community Based Organisations (CBOs), social workers, and other community members involved in community based child protection mechanisms.- CSOs and CBOs: Local child protection organisations support and implement activities at community level, L&A towards national actors, and provide synergies of interventions.- Local and national governments: formulate, endorse and implement laws and public policies related to SEC- Private Sector: Travel and tourism orgs (e.g., large and small, hotels, transport), as well as ICT/ Digital Service Providers have interest to avoid SEC taking place within their value chain, and to avoid having their products and services used to facilitate SEC- International donors, Intergovernmental bodies, INGOs, Multilateral entities55: Targeted audiences and partners for evidence based regional and international lobbying- Dutch Stakeholders: NL Embassies in programme countries, MoFA, MoJ&S, to formalise the network for sustainable cooperation to end SEC and impunity of offenders. The Dutch Public- Media & Journalists: Investigative and reporting outlets in the Programme countries. Media and journalists in the Netherlands.

This group is composed by children from educational units in the urban and peri-urban areas of Cobán, Alta Verapaz. The boys are between 7 and 12 years old and adolescents between 13 and 16 years old, most of them from the Mayan Q'eqch'i ethnic group and the rest mestizo. These boys, who attend local schools, come from families living in poverty and extreme poverty. They will receive education on SRHR and on SEC as a crime that affects their physical, mental and emotional health..

119 male adolescents between 13 and 17 years old and 81 boys between 7 and 12 years old participated, 59% self-identified with the Mayan Q'eqchì' ethnicity and 41% with the mestizo ethnicity. In the attendance registration forms there is a section for the person to write down how he/she identifies him/herself. They attend schools in the urban and peri-urban area of Cobán in Alta Verapaz. They come from families living in poverty and extreme poverty. We have addressed the issues of SRHR and SEC, being a crime that has consequences for their physical, mental and emotional health. It was important to address their SRHR, getting boys to ensure that they have control and autonomy over their own sexuality and reproduction, free from coercion, discrimination and violence. We have emphasised the relationship between SEC and SRHR, as SEC violates this fundamental right. When children are sexually exploited, they are denied their autonomy and their ability to make informed decisions about their sexual health, deprived of their right to healthy and safe sexuality, and denied access to appropriate sexual health services.

We worked with 125 boys aged between 7 and 12 from San Cristobal, who participated in the Boys' School. The participants come from urban and peri-urban areas and are mostly from the Poqomchí Maya ethnic group. The topics covered included ESNNA and DSR. These sessions were held with the informed consent of the parents, as well as with the approval of the school principal and teachers, thus allowing us to provide a comprehensive education adapted to the needs of the context. We also worked with 75 boys aged between 7 and 17 from the Q'eqchi' Mayan ethnic group, so the workshops were facilitated in their mother tongue to ensure cultural and linguistic understanding.

Most of them belong to the Poqomchí Maya ethnic group and are between 13 and 17 years old. The topics of ESNNA and DSDR are relevant to adolescents, taking into account the current contexts of violence, devices and information to which they have access; being informed helps to prevent and avoid the vulnerability of the participants. We also worked with 75 girls aged between 7 and 17 from Lanquin, who belong to the Q'eqchi‘ Mayan ethnic group. Due to the cultural context, the topics were presented in their mother tongue, Q'eqchi’. In order to carry out these sessions, we obtained prior informed consent from parents, as topics such as ESNNA and lDSDR are still considered taboo in many communities. Despite this, we were able to create a safe and respectful space that allowed for dialogue and reflection.

El Refugio de la Niñez carried out institutional lobbying activities aimed at strengthening advocacy for the rights of children and adolescents. These activities focused on establishing and strengthening formal relationships with key public institutions through coordination meetings and participation in inter-institutional forums (Public Prosecutor's Network, Youth Roundtable, VET Network, Ministry of Education).

"El Refugio de la Niñez, partner DTZ is an NGO recognised for its work on behalf of children and adolescents. Through its various programmes, it has coverage in several departments of the country, from where it promotes advocacy and lobbying actions with key decision-makers, the protection system, the judicial system, NGOs, international organisations, local actors and organised civil society. It also has the recognition and capacity to carry out advocacy actions at the national level.The desired future capacity is to continue growing institutionally to provide attention to more people, through advocacy processes based on programmatic quality and relations with international and governmental cooperation to access international and national funds. "

Refugio de la Niñez is a highly credible organisation in Guatemala that works with institutions in the protection system at different levels: national, departmental, municipal and local, establishing strategic alliances with different actors such as the Ministry of Education. The Ministry of Health and municipalities, through their offices for children, adolescents, women and youth, have achieved greater coverage with different activities, encouraging each of them to assume their role in prevention and protection. Within the framework of the project, the establishment of joint actions to achieve the established objectives has been key, in addition to preparing the conditions for the sustainability of the processes. A dialogue was held with community leaders from the urban and peri-urban areas of the municipality of San Cristóbal Verapaz, together with children representing the Escuela de Varones (Boys' School).
